EVERY DECEMBER, Bob and Peggy ask how much of Bob's traditional IRA to convert to a Roth. This year a $25,000 conversion would cost them nearly $17,000 in tax and lost health insurance help. A $130,000 conversion would cost far less per dollar. And the cheapest version of that same conversion isn't available this year at all.
Bob is 66 and on Medicare. Peggy is 64 and buys her coverage on the marketplace until Medicare starts in January. They live in Florida, so state income tax isn't a factor. Their income is $34,000 of Social Security, a $26,000 pension and $10,000 of interest.
The IRA holds about $2 million, which is why they're asking at all. Left alone, it produces required withdrawals from Bob's 75th birthday on, stacked on top of his Social Security. If Peggy outlives him, she'll pay tax on those withdrawals as a single filer. They have savings outside the IRA to pay any conversion tax.
The cliff nearer the ground
The enhanced marketplace subsidies expired at the end of 2025. For 2026, a household of two loses its subsidy entirely once income exceeds $84,600, or 400% of the federal poverty line. Peggy's subsidy pays roughly $12,300 of a benchmark plan that averages about $19,200 a year for a 64-year-old in Florida.
The marketplace counts income its own way, adding back the untaxed part of Bob's Social Security. That puts them at exactly $70,000, with $14,600 of room.
Three conversions
Bob and Peggy start by considering a $12,000 conversion, which keeps them under the line. It adds $2,364 of federal income tax, nearly 20%, even though none of their income is taxed above 12%. Why? The conversion also makes more of Bob's Social Security taxable.
Peggy's subsidy shrinks as well, by $1,195. Add it all up and the $12,000 conversion costs $3,559, or nearly 30%.
Next they consider $25,000. Their federal tax rises to $4,530, but they've crossed the cliff and lost Peggy's entire $12,264 subsidy. Their total cost jumps to $16,794, or 67% of the conversion.
The real danger is stopping just past the line. A $14,500 conversion stays below it, and a $14,700 conversion crosses it. Those extra $200 add about $10,900 of cost, more than $54 per dollar. In fact, the $14,700 conversion costs more than the $14,700 converted.
But something surprising happens when they try a much larger conversion. At $130,000, their federal tax reaches $23,148, including the effect of phasing out part of Bob's new senior deduction. Peggy's subsidy is already gone, so it can't disappear again. Their total cost of $35,412 is 27.2%, less per dollar than the cautious $12,000 conversion and far less than the $25,000 one.
The cliff everyone watches
Medicare has a cliff too. Income in 2026 sets Medicare premiums for 2028, when both of them will be enrolled. Using this year's thresholds and surcharges as a guide, the first surcharge would begin at a conversion of about $153,000. Converting $200 more than that would add roughly $2,300 to the couple's Medicare premiums for that one year. The 2028 figures haven't been published, and the actual amounts may differ.
The Medicare surcharge falls on both of them, while the marketplace subsidy covers only Peggy. Yet the marketplace cliff costs nearly five times as much. It also sits far lower, right where a cautious conversion runs into it.
Cheaper isn't the same as worth it
None of this says Bob and Peggy should convert $130,000. It says the cost doesn't climb in a straight line, and the amount that feels prudent can be the most expensive per dollar.
Whether a conversion makes sense depends on how its total cost today, taxes and lost benefits included, compares with what those dollars would cost when eventually withdrawn from the IRA. Those later withdrawals carry their own tax, and they can raise Social Security taxation and Medicare premiums too. It also matters where the money to pay today's tax comes from, and what it might otherwise earn. Money that would come out at 22% isn't obviously worth converting at 27%, while money headed for 32% might be.
One more December warning. If Peggy takes the subsidy in advance each month, crossing the cliff means paying it back, and starting this year there's no cap on the repayment.
A different year
In January Peggy moves to Medicare and becomes eligible for the senior tax deductions, and there's no marketplace subsidy left to lose. With the same income, the same $130,000 conversion in 2027 would add about $22,300 of federal tax, or 17.2%.
That's roughly $13,100 less than the same conversion this year. It compares today's costs, not lifetime results, and future taxes and investment growth still matter. But the option Bob and Peggy hadn't considered wasn't a different amount. It was a different year.
December is the last chance to look harder at this tax year, and Bob and Peggy's numbers show why a glance at the brackets isn't enough. The cliffs are different for every household, and the costliest one isn't always the one we're watching.

John Urban is the founder of RetireSmartIRA, a retirement tax-planning app. Earlier, he founded GT Nexus, a supply-chain software company acquired by Infor in 2015. He lives in Northern California with his wife, Kathy, and enjoys time with family, travel, reading, Bay Area sports, and the occasional deep dive into the fine print of the tax code.
